paragraphs.text: Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair is a RASopathy with Noonan syndrome-like features and distinctive ectodermal abnormalities (Motta et al., 2019). Mazzanti et al. (2003) described the condition as combining a facial appearance not completely typical of Noonan syndrome, a behavioral phenotype, growth hormone (GH) deficiency, darkly pigmented hairless skin, and loose anagen hair. Cordeddu et al. (2009) found that affected individuals had reduced growth, often with proven GH deficiency, cognitive deficits, distinctive hyperactive behavior that improved with age in most of them, and easily pluckable, sparse, thin, slow-growing hair.

checks.evidence_quote: A recurrent activating mutation in SHOC2 (p.Ser2Gly) causes Mazzanti syndrome, a RASopathy characterized by features resembling Noonan syndrome and distinctive ectodermal abnormalities.
checks.explanation: Mazzanti syndrome is the same disorder as Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair, and the abstract describes it exactly this way.

paragraphs.text: Tosti et al. (1991) reported a 4.5-year-old girl with loose anagen hair and Noonan syndrome. She had short, blond, easily pluckable hair that had never been cut. paragraphs.text: Tosti et al. (1997) reported 19 patients with loose anagen hair (14 children and 5 adults). Associated conditions included Noonan syndrome in a 5-year-old boy. In all patients the trichogram showed a predominance of anagen hairs (80 to 100%) devoid of sheaths. The authors concluded that loose anagen hair may be sporadic, may occur together with developmental or acquired conditions, or, less often, may be familial.

paragraphs.text: Cordeddu et al. (2009) studied 25 sporadic subjects with a relatively consistent phenotype previously termed Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair, all carrying the same SHOC2 mutation. They had facial features typical of Noonan syndrome, reduced growth frequently associated with proven GH deficiency, cognitive deficits, distinctive hyperactive behavior that improved with age in most, a hypernasal voice, and hair anomalies including easily pluckable, sparse, thin, slow-growing hair; loose anagen hair was confirmed microscopically in 12. Some had darkly pigmented skin, eczema, or ichthyosis, and facial and other features variably included macrocephaly, high forehead, hypertelorism, palpebral ptosis, low-set posteriorly rotated ears, short or webbed neck, and pectus anomalies. Mitral valve dysplasia and septal defects were significantly overrepresented compared with the general Noonan syndrome population. Referring pediatricians felt that several subjects had features suggestive of Costello or cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome as newborns or young infants, and the phenotype combined features from across the neuro-cardio-facial-cutaneous disorders family.

paragraphs.text: Komatsuzaki et al. (2010) reported 8 patients with the SHOC2 S2G mutation. All had short stature, sparse hair, and atopic skin; 6 had severe mental retardation and easily pluckable hair, and 1 had leukocytosis. paragraphs.text: Hoban et al. (2012) reported a male infant with the SHOC2 S2G mutation who presented with fetal distress requiring premature delivery at 32 weeks. He had dysmorphic features, edema, hepatosplenomegaly, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and respiratory distress after birth. Echocardiography showed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with left ventricular outflow tract obstruction; the cardiac lesion rapidly progressed, and he was discharged home for palliative care. The authors noted that the cardiac findings and features were atypical compared with previously reported individuals with this mutation and concluded that the case expanded the phenotype to include fetal distress and fatal hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in a premature infant.

paragraphs.text: Gripp et al. (2013) reported 5 male patients with the SHOC2 S2G mutation. Patient 1 had prenatal polyhydramnios, cystic hygroma, and macrosomia, followed by pyloric stenosis, severe feeding difficulties and failure to thrive requiring gastrostomy, mild pulmonic valve stenosis, axial hypotonia, small optic nerves, delayed motor development, macrocephaly (OFC +3 SD) with a large anterior fontanel and dolichocephaly, sparse thin hair, long eyelashes, bilateral ptosis, downslanting palpebral fissures, hepatosplenomegaly, hemangiomas, and fine wrinkling of the hands. Bone marrow biopsies showed markedly hypercellular marrow with increased reticulin staining consistent with myelofibrosis, and blasts were present in peripheral blood; he died at age 2.5 years after splenectomy in preparation for bone marrow transplantation. Patient 2 had polyhydramnios, increased birth weight, severe feeding difficulties, macrocephaly, unilateral ptosis, posteriorly angulated ears, increased wrinkling of the palms, loose skin, bilateral inguinal hernias, and hypotonia, so that Costello syndrome was considered; he had a subdural effusion requiring drainage, intellectual disability with independent walking at age 5 years and a few single words at 9 years, short stature, acanthosis nigricans, and eczema. Patient 3 had polyhydramnios and fetal macrosomia, tracheostenosis, chronic lung disease, a neonatal seizure, right bundle branch block, biventricular hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, aortic insufficiency, mild pulmonic stenosis, and failure to thrive requiring gastrostomy; Costello syndrome was suggested clinically. At age 9 years his height was 125 cm (10th centile), weight 29.4 kg (50th centile), and OFC 60 cm (+5 SD), and he was diagnosed with pervasive developmental disorder and Tourette syndrome. Patient 4, of Mexican ancestry, had poor growth, atrial septal defect, patent foramen ovale, trivial mitral regurgitation, severe eczema, poorly growing, easily pluckable blond hair much lighter than that of his family, very long eyelashes, mild to moderate intellectual disability, and no macrocephaly; brain MRI showed mild ventriculomegaly and subependymal heterotopia, and MRI at 6 years for headaches showed development of a Chiari I malformation in the context of platybasia and basilar invagination, with C3-C4 vertebral fusion. Patient 5 had neonatal hypotonia, feeding difficulties requiring a nasogastric tube, patent ductus arteriosus, an abnormal mitral valve with 3 papillary muscles and redundant chordae, short stature, macrocephaly (OFC +2 SD), attention deficit disorder, and a duplicated renal collecting system; his hair grew slowly and had never been cut, but he never had hair loss or easily pluckable hair.

They described distinctive brain abnormalities, including relative megalencephaly with enlarged subarachnoid spaces suggestive of benign external hydrocephalus and a relatively small posterior fossa indicated by a vertical tentorium, and suggested that this combination likely accounted for the high rate of cerebellar tonsillar ectopia and postnatally developed Chiari I malformation; including literature cases, 3 of 8 patients with MRI had a Chiari I malformation. The myelofibrosis in patient 1 was the first hematologic neoplasm reported with the SHOC2 mutation.

paragraphs.text: Cordeddu et al. (2009) used in silico protein network analysis seeded with known RAS-MAPK disease proteins to rank candidate Noonan syndrome genes, and resequenced the top candidate, SHOC2, in 96 mutation-negative Noonan syndrome patients. They found a heterozygous c.4A-G transition, resulting in a ser2-to-gly (S2G) substitution, in 4 unrelated individuals. Among a further 410 mutation-negative subjects with Noonan syndrome or a related phenotype, 21 had the same change; no other disease-associated SHOC2 variant was found. The mutation was absent in the parents and de novo in the families with parental DNA available (3 of the 4 in the first cohort and 12 in the second), with paternity confirmed. Detection of the mutation in DNA from several tissues indicated that it was a germline mutation. Functional studies showed that the S2G substitution created an N-myristoylation site: SHOC2(S2G), but not wildtype SHOC2 or a disease-unrelated S2A mutant, took up [3H]-myristic acid in Cos-1 cells. Wildtype SHOC2 was distributed through the cytoplasm and nucleus in starved cells and moved to the nucleus after EGF stimulation, whereas SHOC2(S2G) was targeted to the cell membrane in both conditions; an N-myristoyltransferase inhibitor reduced or abolished membrane localization, but the mutant still did not translocate to the nucleus. Wildtype and mutant SHOC2 did not heterodimerize, ruling out a dominant-negative effect through sequestration of the wildtype protein, and SHOC2(S2G) increased EGF-dependent ERK phosphorylation in Neuro2A neuroblastoma cells but not in Cos-1 or 293T cells, indicating cell type-specific MAPK activation.

paragraphs.text: In a 5-year-old girl of European ancestry with a mild RASopathy and her father, Hannig et al. (2014) identified a heterozygous c.519G-A transition in the SHOC2 gene, resulting in a met173-to-ile (M173I) substitution. The parents were not consanguineous. Both carriers had features overlapping Noonan syndrome, cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome, and Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair. The variant was not found in 6,500 asymptomatic individuals. In SHOC2-depleted Cos1 cells, the M173I mutant restored EGF-induced ERK1/2 phosphorylation by only about 10% above basal, whereas wildtype SHOC2 fully rescued it; protein half-life, subcellular localization, and binding to M-RAS and RAF-1 were unchanged. The mutant failed to precipitate endogenous PP1c effectively and supported only a mild EGF-induced increase in RAF-1 ser338 phosphorylation, and the authors concluded that reduced SHOC2-PP1c binding causes loss of function in the ERK1/2 pathway.

paragraphs.text: Motta et al. (2019) reported a c.807_808delinsTT change in the SHOC2 gene, resulting in a gln269_his270delinshis-tyr (Q269_H270delinsHY) change, associated with prenatal-onset hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The mutant bound more strongly to MRAS and PPP1CB and increased MAPK signaling, indicating an activating effect, but unlike S2G it was not constitutively targeted to the plasma membrane.
